title: SaaS Billing Models Explained: Flat-Rate, Per-User, Tiered and Usage-Based Pricing
summary: Understand the main SaaS billing models, their benefits, limitations and ideal use cases, with practical pricing examples for each model.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


SaaS billing models define how software companies charge customers for access, features and usage. The right model connects price to customer value while keeping bills understandable and revenue reasonably predictable.


Choosing between flat-rate, per-user, tiered, usage-based, freemium, credit-based and hybrid billing affects more than pricing. It shapes acquisition, expansion revenue, churn, cash flow and the complexity of your billing system.


### TL;DR


Use flat-rate billing for simplicity, per-user pricing when value grows with team size, tiered pricing for distinct customer segments, and usage-based billing when consumption reflects value. Freemium can support product-led acquisition, while credits help customers control variable spend. Many SaaS businesses eventually combine models to balance predictable revenue with expansion.

##


How SaaS Subscription Billing Supports Different Pricing Models


A pricing model decides what a customer owes. A subscription billing system determines when and how that amount is collected. It usually needs to manage billing cycles, trials, upgrades, downgrades, cancellations, proration, invoices and failed-payment recovery.


For recurring collections in India, businesses may also need cards,[UPI AutoPay](https://www.cashfree.com/upi-autopay/) and[eNACH mandates](https://www.cashfree.com/enach/) . A flexible[recurring payment solution](https://www.cashfree.com/recurring-payment/) should support the chosen pricing model without making the payment experience difficult for customers.


### 1. Flat-Rate SaaS Billing: One Product, One Price


Flat-rate billing gives every customer the same product at one fixed monthly or annual price. There are no seats, consumption meters or multiple plans to calculate.


For example, a project management tool may charge ₹2,999 per month for unlimited users and projects. A five-person startup and a 50-person agency pay the same amount.


**Advantages:** It is easy to explain, sell and administer. Revenue per account is predictable, and the model suits an early product with a narrow use case.


**Limitations:** It does not capture differences in customer size or value. Small customers may find the price high, while larger customers can receive much more value without contributing additional revenue. Upsell options are also limited.


**Best suited for:** Focused products whose value and cost do not vary greatly between customers.


### 2. Per-User SaaS Billing: Pricing by Seats


Per-user, or seat-based, billing charges according to the number of people who can access the software. A CRM priced at ₹800 per user per month would cost ₹8,000 for ten users and ₹40,000 for 50 users.


**Advantages:** Pricing is easy to understand, and revenue expands as a customer adds employees or departments. It works well when each additional user receives clear value.


**Limitations:** Customers may restrict seats, share logins or delay wider adoption to control costs. The model can be a poor fit when a product becomes more valuable through company-wide access.


**Best suited for:** CRM, HR, collaboration and productivity products where value broadly increases with active users.


### 3. Tiered SaaS Pricing: Plans Based on Features and Limits


Tiered pricing offers several plans with different features, limits or support levels. Customers select the closest fit and move to a higher plan as their needs grow.


A marketing platform might offer Starter at ₹4,999 per month for 5,000 contacts, Growth at ₹14,999 for 25,000 contacts and advanced workflows, and Enterprise with custom limits and support.


**Advantages:** Tiers serve different customer segments and create a visible upgrade path. Price increases can be tied to additional capacity or capabilities.


**Limitations:** Packaging requires care. Too many plans create decision friction, while gating one important feature behind a costly tier can frustrate customers.


**Best suited for:** Products with customer groups that differ naturally by company size, feature requirements or usage limits.

### 4. Usage-Based SaaS Billing: Pricing by Consumption


Usage-based, metered or consumption-based billing charges customers for what they consume. Common meters include API calls, storage, compute time, messages, transactions and AI tokens.


The model may be fully variable or include a base subscription with an allowance and overage charges. For example, an API platform could include one million calls in a monthly plan and charge for additional blocks of calls.


**Advantages:** Price can track value closely, lowers the entry barrier for smaller customers and allows revenue to expand as product use increases.


**Limitations:** Monthly revenue and customer bills are less predictable. Accurate metering, real-time usage visibility, alerts and clear invoices are essential. A technically convenient metric is not always a meaningful value metric.


**Best suited for:** Infrastructure, data, communications, API and AI products with wide variation in customer consumption.


### How to Choose a SaaS Value Metric


Customers should be able to understand the unit, estimate their likely bill and connect higher usage with greater value. If they cannot, usage-based pricing can feel unpredictable rather than fair.


### 5. Freemium SaaS Model: Free Access With Paid Upgrades


Freemium gives customers ongoing access to a limited product at no charge. Users upgrade when they need more storage, seats, usage or advanced features. Unlike a free trial, the free plan does not expire.


**Advantages:** Prospects can experience the product before paying, and the free tier can support product-led acquisition or network effects.


**Limitations:** Free users still create infrastructure and support costs. If the free plan offers too much, conversion suffers; if it offers too little, users may never reach the product’s core value.


**Best suited for:** Self-serve software with fast time to value, low cost per free user and a clear reason to upgrade.


### 6. Credit-Based SaaS Billing: Prepaid Usage


In credit-based billing, customers purchase a balance and spend credits when they use the service. An AI tool might sell 10,000 credits for ₹5,000 and deduct a defined number for each generation or processing task.


**Advantages:** The business collects revenue upfront, while customers can cap spending and top up when required. It handles intermittent or bursty usage well.


**Limitations:** The conversion between money, credits and delivered value must be clear. Expiry rules, unused balances and changing credit costs can create distrust. The product also needs balance tracking, low-balance alerts and optional automatic recharges.


**Best suited for:** AI tools, messaging services and data platforms where usage is variable but customers want prepaid control.


### 7. Hybrid SaaS Pricing: Combining Subscription and Usage Charges


Hybrid pricing combines two or more models. Common structures include:


- A base subscription plus usage overages
- A tiered plan with additional per-user charges
- A fixed platform fee plus metered premium features
- An annual commitment with prepaid credits


Hybrid models can provide a dependable revenue floor while allowing expansion as customers add users or consume more. However, every added component makes quoting, metering and invoicing harder. Use a hybrid model only when each charge maps to a distinct source of value.


##


How to Choose the Best SaaS Billing Model for Your Product


Start with how customers receive value, not with what competitors charge.


1. **Identify the value metric.** Is value driven by access, seats, transactions, storage, outcomes or another measurable unit?
2. **Review usage variation.** Similar usage across accounts may support flat-rate pricing. Wide variation points towards tiers, credits or metering.
3. **Test predictability.** Customers should be able to estimate their bill, while the company should be able to forecast revenue and delivery costs.
4. **Check expansion paths.** Decide whether growth should come from more seats, higher limits, premium features or greater consumption.
5. **Assess billing complexity.** Metering, proration, tax, retries and reconciliation can make a theoretically strong model expensive to operate.
6. **Validate with customer data.** Model the change against real accounts before altering packaging or prices.


The billing model can evolve. A SaaS company may begin with flat-rate pricing, introduce tiers after customer segments become clearer, and later add usage charges for costly features.

##


Which SaaS Billing Model Should You Choose?


There is no universally best SaaS billing model. Flat-rate pricing offers simplicity, per-user billing links revenue to team growth, tiers serve distinct segments, and usage-based pricing tracks consumption. Freemium supports acquisition, while credits give customers control over irregular usage.


Choose the simplest model that reflects how customers receive value and still covers the cost of serving them. Add complexity only when it creates a clearer price-to-value relationship. Whatever the model, reliable recurring collections, transparent invoices and accurate reconciliation determine whether it works in practice.

##


Frequently Asked Questions


#### What are the most common SaaS billing models?


The main SaaS billing models are flat-rate, per-user, tiered, usage-based, freemium, credit-based and hybrid pricing. The right choice depends on how customers receive value and how much their usage varies.


#### What is usage-based billing in SaaS?


Usage-based billing charges customers according to a measurable unit such as API calls, transactions, storage, compute time or tokens. It is also called metered or consumption-based billing.


#### What is the difference between tiered and per-user pricing?


Tiered pricing charges for a package of features or limits. Per-user pricing changes according to the number of seats. A business can combine both by setting a price per seat within each plan.


#### Is freemium the same as a free trial?


No. A free trial expires after a fixed period, while a freemium plan remains available with defined limits. Both aim to let users experience the product before purchasing.


#### When should a SaaS company use hybrid pricing?


Hybrid pricing is useful when one metric cannot represent the full value delivered. A stable platform fee can cover baseline access, while seat or usage charges capture expansion.


#### Can SaaS billing models be changed later?


Yes, but existing contracts, customer communication, migration rules and billing-system capabilities must be considered. Test a new model with a limited segment before a broad rollout.
